purpose: Pre-submission hostile-but-fair Q1 peer reviewer simulation: current risks and artifact-backed responses. Reconciled against the 207-row canonical panel and current manuscript/artifacts on 2026-11-16. Current counts and metrics must be read from the cited artifacts; unresolved permissions and author/editor decisions remain open.

top_risk_areas: Thin effective support for multi-parameter tiers
No established predictive advantage over the linear baseline
Restricted inputs and derived-panel redistribution review
Country-level high-error cases and untested joint exclusion

criticisms.title: Temporal extrapolation remains limited under rolling-origin validation
criticisms.criticism: Forward-chaining rolling-origin validation spans only 25 folds, and 95% interval coverage averages 86.7%, 84.5%, and 81.7% for Tiers A, B, and C; 36%, 48%, and 48% of folds, respectively, fall below nominal coverage. Some fold-level R² values are negative. The evidence therefore does not establish reliable temporal extrapolation.
artifact_evidence: cv_rolling_origin.json — 25 forward-chaining folds with fold-level metrics
prediction_interval_coverage.json — mean rolling-origin coverage A/B/C=86.7%/84.5%/81.7%; below-nominal fold rates=36%/48%/48%
criticisms.rebuttal: We agree that the current evidence does not validate temporal extrapolation. Repeated grouped k-fold is the primary spatial validation protocol; country-out is a separate stress test, and rolling-origin is a temporal scope diagnostic. The manuscript reports the current 25-fold coverage and its variability and does not use rolling-origin as evidence for temporal forecasting. More temporal observations or a redesigned model would be needed to establish forward transport.
corrective_actions: Manuscript explicitly reports rolling-origin undercoverage rates (Section 7, supplementary Table S5)
Prediction interval coverage artifact upgraded to protocol-tier stratification (v2)
Discussion Limitations section identifies temporal extrapolation as unsupported inference
Tier C excluded from headline claims precisely because of temporal fragility
criticisms.resolution_note: Partially addressed through explicit reporting and scope limits. Temporal extrapolation remains unsupported by the current 25-fold evidence.

criticisms.title: Thin effective support constrains multi-parameter inference
criticisms.criticism: The canonical panel has 207 unique country-year rows across 83 countries. The nominal tier sizes are 11, 18 and 22 parameters, corresponding to 18.82, 11.50 and 9.41 observations per parameter. Several channel terms are withdrawn and neutralized to zero. How should readers interpret the higher-order tiers when support is thin and some nominal terms are not estimated?
artifact_evidence: model_complexity_support.json — Tier A/B/C: 18.82 / 11.50 / 9.41 observations per nominal parameter; A/B primary, C exploratory
model_ladder_metrics.json — parameter counts 11 / 18 / 22; Tier C inferentialRole=exploratory
tier_b_stability_sweep.json — 83 country-out folds; x_safe sign consistency 0.759, below the 0.80 Tier B threshold
criticisms.rebuttal: The support ratios use the nominal tier parameter counts and describe design complexity, not identification of each coefficient. Tier A/B are the primary complexity tiers; Tier C is exploratory. The current Tier B country-out stability summary has 83 folds and a minimum sign-consistency value of 0.759 for x_safe, below the stated 0.80 threshold. That summary includes neutralized channel entries and does not establish that every term is identified. Thin support and weak identification remain limitations.
corrective_actions: Tiered complexity ladder with explicit support-per-parameter ratios (model_complexity_support.json)
Tier C excluded from headline claims (model_ladder_metrics.json inferentialRole=exploratory)
Manuscript Discussion §8.1 states effective support units and constraints explicitly
Support envelope card in app UI with visible regime coverage diagnostics
criticisms.resolution_note: Partially mitigated through explicit tier roles, current support ratios, and a flagged Tier B term. Thin support and weak identification remain substantive limitations; the manuscript does not claim that the full 18- or 22-parameter structure is identified.

criticisms.title: Prediction intervals do not attain nominal coverage in every protocol
criticisms.criticism: The nominal 95% intervals show below-nominal mean coverage and substantial fold-to-fold variation, especially under rolling-origin. Reporting 95% intervals risks implying calibration that the observed results do not establish. How are these intervals to be interpreted?
artifact_evidence: prediction_interval_coverage.json — protocol- and tier-specific coverage, fold variability, and below-nominal fold rates
cv_rolling_origin.json and cv_country_out.json — fold-level evaluation results
criticisms.rebuttal: The intervals are uncertainty summaries, not a guarantee of 95% coverage. In country-out folds, mean coverage is 91.6%/91.4%/90.8% for Tiers A/B/C; under rolling-origin it is 86.7%/84.5%/81.7%, with 36%/48%/48% of folds below nominal. The manuscript reports protocol-specific coverage and variability and limits interpretation accordingly. These results do not establish universally calibrated prediction intervals.
corrective_actions: prediction_interval_coverage.json upgraded to v2 with stratified gap-to-nominal diagnostics
Manuscript calibration language revised (Prompt 7) — no overstatement of coverage
Supplementary Table S5 reports exact undercoverage fractions by protocol × tier
Discussion acknowledges rolling-origin failure explicitly
criticisms.resolution_note: Partially addressed through protocol-specific reporting and calibrated interpretation. Nominal coverage is not attained consistently, particularly across rolling-origin folds.

criticisms.title: WVS microdata redistribution blocks full replication
criticisms.criticism: The paper claims a reproducible open-science workflow, but the core outcome variable Z is derived from World Values Survey microdata that cannot be legally redistributed. A replicator cannot regenerate results from the repository alone. This fundamentally undermines the reproducibility claim.
artifact_evidence: data_code_provenance.json — WVS/EVS sources flagged as redistribution-restricted (4 sources)
REPLICATION_RUNBOOK.md — § 9 Data Provenance documents restriction
criticisms.rebuttal: The repository contains a derived country-year panel and runbook instructions, but upstream WVS/EVS data remain redistribution-restricted and are absent from a clean checkout. A clean clone therefore cannot independently rebuild all inputs. The right to redistribute the derived panel also remains under review; this response does not assert that the panel or every analysis artifact is legally redistributable. The runbook and provenance inventory improve traceability, but source access and redistribution permission remain open gates.
corrective_actions: Provenance inventory records source-specific restrictions and unresolved review items
REPLICATION_RUNBOOK documents required inputs, hashes, and retrieval steps
Clean-clone rebuild limitations and derived-panel redistribution review remain open
criticisms.resolution_note: Partially mitigated through documentation and provenance. Full clean-clone regeneration and redistribution clearance remain unresolved; do not describe the derived panel as cleared for redistribution.

criticisms.title: Scenario replication formerly inflated the apparent sample size (resolved in v2)
criticisms.criticism: An earlier version of this work reported n=630 observations that arose from redistribution scenario replication of a much smaller set of unique country-year cells, which would have made standard errors, test statistics and fit metrics systematically over-optimistic. Does the current analysis still depend on that inflation?
artifact_evidence: metrics_authoritative.json — n=207, dataset_id=public/data/panel_canonical_v2.csv
model_complexity_support.json — nUniqueCountryYears=207, equal to the row count
public/data/panel_canonical_v2.csv — 207 rows, 83 countries, 1990-2023, no scenario column
criticisms.rebuttal: The earlier 630-row scenario panel is retired. The current canonical panel has 207 rows and 207 distinct country-year keys across 83 countries. The panel audit and model-complexity artifact record those counts. Current validation includes 83 country-out folds and 100 repeated grouped k-fold evaluations; the country is kept intact within each grouped fold. The correction is disclosed in the supplementary note.
corrective_actions: Retired the 630-row scenario panel; canonical panel has 207 complete-case country-years
Canonical row count equals the 207 unique (iso3, year) keys
Validation artifacts record 83 country-out folds and 100 grouped k-fold evaluations
Sample change disclosed in the supplementary correction note
criticisms.resolution_note: Resolved by correction, not by argument: the scenario panel is gone and the analysed row count now equals the unique count.

criticisms.title: Infinite VIF for D and S variables suggests collinearity problems
criticisms.criticism: The supplementary VIF diagnostics show infinite variance inflation factors for variables D (social atomization) and S (social support). Infinite VIF indicates perfect or near-perfect collinearity, which makes coefficient estimates for these variables unidentifiable. How can the authors interpret coefficients of collinear predictors?
artifact_evidence: rawdata/wvs_construct_audit.json — D alpha=-1.23, S computable in 0 cells
model_ladder_metrics.json — 7 estimated columns; C, D, G, S neutralised
Supplementary Table S10 — VIF diagnostics: D=Inf, S=Inf (legacy full-feature path)
criticisms.rebuttal: The construct audit found D internally inconsistent (alpha=-1.2285) and S uncomputable in any country-year under the configured item requirement. These constructs are withdrawn from substantive interpretation; their legacy/full-feature VIF diagnostics remain as an audit trail. The paper does not interpret coefficients for withdrawn channels.
corrective_actions: Construct audit documents D reliability failure and S computability failure
D and S are withdrawn from substantive interpretation alongside C and G
Legacy VIF diagnostics are labeled as diagnostics for the earlier full-feature specification
criticisms.resolution_note: Resolved by withdrawal rather than by interpretation: the collinear channels no longer enter the estimated design matrix.

criticisms.title: No formal model selection criteria (AIC/BIC) — tier choice appears ad hoc
criticisms.criticism: The paper presents three model tiers (A, B, C) of increasing complexity but provides no formal model selection criterion (AIC, BIC, cross-validated deviance, Bayes factor) to justify the tier hierarchy. The tier labels appear to be imposed by the authors rather than derived from data. What prevents adding or removing tiers arbitrarily?
artifact_evidence: model_ladder_metrics.json — tier A/B/C definitions with param counts but no IC scores
model_complexity_support.json — complexity vs support analysis
criticisms.rebuttal: The tier ladder is reported as a nested complexity comparison, not as a formally selected optimum. Tier A contains the baseline terms, Tier B adds interactions, and Tier C adds curvature for exploratory sensitivity. The manuscript uses repeated grouped k-fold as its primary spatial evaluation, with country-out and rolling-origin results reported separately. No AIC/BIC or other formal selection criterion is claimed; whether this descriptive ladder is sufficient for a particular venue remains an editorial question.
corrective_actions: Manuscript describes the tier ladder and its interpretation boundaries
Repeated grouped k-fold is identified as the primary spatial evaluation; other protocols are scoped separately
No claim of formal model selection is made; venue-level adequacy remains open
criticisms.resolution_note: Partially addressed by stating that the tiers are a descriptive complexity ladder rather than a selected optimum. Absence of a formal selection criterion remains a limitation.

criticisms.title: Ridge at Z=0.5 is a mathematical artifact, not an empirical discovery
criticisms.criticism: The paper emphasizes a 'transition ridge at Z=0.5' as a substantive finding, but this is simply the inflection point of the logistic function S/(S+k) — it will always occur at Z=0.5 by construction regardless of the data. Calling this an empirical result is misleading.
artifact_evidence: Method Section (Eq. 3) — saturation transform has inflection at Z=0.5 by definition
model_ladder_metrics.json — ridge referenced in interpretation
criticisms.rebuttal: This is a fair and important point, and the manuscript is already careful about it. The ridge at Z=0.5 is indeed a structural feature of the chosen functional form (logistic/Hill saturation), not an empirically discovered threshold. The manuscript states this explicitly: 'the transition ridge at Z=0.5 separating low-uptake and high-uptake regimes in the model-implied geometry' (Discussion §8.2) and 'These regime-dependent movements are features of the fitted function, not predictions of real-world policy responses' (Conclusion). The contribution is not discovering the ridge but (1) showing that empirical data populate both sides of the ridge with interpretable regime structure, and (2) demonstrating that sensitivity analysis conditional on regime location yields more informative marginal effects than global averages. The ridge is a lens, not a finding.
corrective_actions: Discussion explicitly labels ridge as 'model-implied geometry' not empirical finding
Conclusion states regime movements are 'features of the fitted function'
Marginal effects reported as model-conditional, not causal
criticisms.resolution_note: Already addressed in manuscript language. The ridge is presented as a structural feature of the chosen model form, not as an empirical discovery.

criticisms.title: C-exclusion sensitivity is non-informative after construct withdrawal
criticisms.criticism: In the rebuilt design, C is withdrawn and neutralized to a constant. Table S18 therefore reports zero change under C exclusion and permutation. That result is non-informative about a substantive C effect. Why retain this sensitivity table instead of removing it?
artifact_evidence: c_dominance_sensitivity.json — nRows=207; C exclusion and permutation produce zero change because C is neutralized
Supplementary Table S18 — explicitly states that the diagnostics do not estimate a substantive contribution of C
marginal_effects.json — C is absent from the retained-channel effects table
criticisms.rebuttal: The table preserves an audit trail for a central defect in the earlier specification, while stating that the rebuilt-panel results cannot estimate a C effect. The artifact records nRows=207 and identical fits after exclusion or permutation because the withdrawn column is constant. The supplementary interpretation boundary calls the diagnostics non-informative by construction; no claim of predictive contribution or robustness for C is made.
corrective_actions: Withdraw C from estimation after the item-level reliability audit
Label Table S18 exclusion and permutation results as non-informative by construction
Remove C from the retained-channel marginal-effects table
Keep the historical identity defect separate from rebuilt-panel evidence
criticisms.resolution_note: Retained as a transparent audit record. Table S18 now explains that a constant withdrawn column cannot establish a substantive C effect; its zero differences are not interpreted as robustness.

criticisms.title: Ecological fallacy: country-year aggregates cannot inform individual-level dynamics
criticisms.criticism: The paper studies country-year level associations between urbanization, inequality, and belief intensity. Robinson (1950) showed long ago that aggregate-level correlations need not reflect individual-level relationships. The paper's implications section hints at policy relevance that cannot be grounded in ecological data. Why should readers care about country-level associations that may not hold for individuals?
artifact_evidence: main.tex Discussion §8.1 — ecological aggregation acknowledged
Supplementary — Table S0 Claim-Evidence Traceability includes ecological inference limits
criticisms.rebuttal: This is acknowledged explicitly and repeatedly as a design boundary, not an oversight. (1) The Discussion §8.1 states: 'the analysis is ecological: the unit is the country-year... aggregate associations need not reflect individual-level mechanisms' and cites Robinson (1950) and Openshaw (1984). (2) Table S0 includes 'Ecological inference limits' as a Tier 0 (study design) claim boundary. (3) The Conclusion explicitly states claims are about 'macro-level regularities in the fitted model, not individual-level behavioral responses'. (4) Policy implications are framed as model-implied counterfactuals on the fitted surface, not predictions of individual behavior changes. The paper's contribution is a macro-level visual analytics framework, not a micro-level causal model — the ecological level is the intended unit of analysis, consistent with macro-urban analytics literature.
corrective_actions: Discussion §8.1 explicitly cites Robinson (1950) and Openshaw (1984)
Table S0 includes ecological inference as a design boundary
Conclusion frames claims as 'macro-level regularities'
Policy implications stated as 'model-implied counterfactuals', not predictions
criticisms.resolution_note: Ecological level is the intended unit of analysis. Limitation is prominently disclosed throughout.

criticisms.title: Tier C instability undermines inclusion in the paper
criticisms.criticism: Tier C has the lowest nominal support ratio (9.41 observations per parameter), greater complexity, and exploratory status. Including it may invite overinterpretation even when it is excluded from headline claims. Why retain it?
artifact_evidence: model_complexity_support.json — Tier C has 22 nominal parameters and 9.41 observations per parameter
model_ladder_metrics.json — Tier C is labeled exploratory and excluded from headline inference
parameter_stability.json and cv_rolling_origin.json — tier-specific stability and validation diagnostics
criticisms.rebuttal: Tier C is retained only as an exploratory sensitivity comparison so readers can inspect the consequences of adding curvature. It is excluded from headline inference, and its estimates are not presented as better-supported results. The lower support ratio and protocol-specific instability remain reasons for caution.
corrective_actions: Tier C is labeled exploratory in the current model-ladder artifact
Manuscript excludes Tier C from headline inferential claims
Support and validation limitations are reported alongside the Tier C comparison
criticisms.resolution_note: Scope is controlled by retaining Tier C only as exploratory sensitivity. Its support limitations remain.

criticisms.title: Tier C adds little in-sample fit relative to its extra complexity
criticisms.criticism: On the current 207-row panel, Tier C raises in-sample R² only from 0.5591 to 0.5634 over Tier B while adding four nominal parameters and reducing support to 9.41 observations per parameter. Why retain it?
artifact_evidence: model_ladder_metrics.json — current in-sample R²: Tier A=0.4623, B=0.5591, C=0.5634
model_complexity_support.json — parameter counts 11/18/22 and support ratios 18.82/11.50/9.41
model_ladder_metrics.json — Tier A/B primary candidates; Tier C exploratory
criticisms.rebuttal: Tier C is retained as a sensitivity appendix, not as a primary inferential tier. Its small incremental in-sample gain over Tier B is disclosed alongside the added nominal terms and lower support ratio. The tier label and interpretation boundary prevent that gain from being presented as a stronger substantive result; primary claims are limited to Tier A/B refit out-of-sample evidence.
corrective_actions: Current in-sample fit and support ratios are reported together
Tier C is explicitly exploratory and excluded from headline inference
No substantive advantage is claimed from the small in-sample increment
criticisms.resolution_note: Resolved by scope control rather than by claiming an advantage: Tier C remains exploratory, and the manuscript reports its small in-sample increment with its lower support ratio.

criticisms.title: Hill/saturation modeling is well-established — novelty claim overstated
criticisms.criticism: Hill-type saturation models date to 1910 and are standard in biochemistry, pharmacology, and ecology. Applying logistic saturation to social survey data is a straightforward application of a known functional form. Where is the genuine methodological novelty beyond standard nonlinear regression with a known link function?
artifact_evidence: main.tex Section 4 — cites Hill (1910), Michaelis-Menten (1913), Briggs-Haldane (1925)
journal_fit_targeting.json — novelty risk flagged for Nature Human Behaviour
criticisms.rebuttal: The manuscript does not claim to introduce the saturation functional form. It frames its contribution as an audit of measurement, design integrity, model comparison, and reproducibility in this application. Whether that contribution clears a journal’s novelty threshold is a venue-level judgment; no claim that the components or their combination are unprecedented is made here.
corrective_actions: Prior art cited prominently in Method section
journal_fit_targeting.json positions paper as 'methodology + workflow' contribution
abstract_screening_pack.json calibrates novelty claims to 'integrative framework'
Title/abstract avoid claiming functional-form novelty
criticisms.resolution_note: Functional-form novelty is not claimed. The paper positions its contribution as an application-specific measurement and reproducibility audit; journal fit remains an editorial decision.

criticisms.title: The complete-case country sample limits generalizability claims
criticisms.criticism: The 83-country complete-case panel is selected by WVS coverage and availability of all required macro covariates. Does this support claims about countries, periods, or contexts outside the observed panel?
artifact_evidence: public/data/panel_canonical_v2.csv — 83 countries, 1990-2023
construct_validity_invariance.json — invariance tested across available countries only
criticisms.rebuttal: The manuscript limits its empirical claims to the observed country-year support and identifies broader geographic and temporal coverage as future work. The panel is not described as globally representative. Its complete-case construction and validation results do not establish transport to unobserved countries or contexts.
corrective_actions: Country-year support and complete-case criteria are documented
Discussion limits claims to observed support and identifies expansion as future work
No population-representative or universal generalization claim is made
criticisms.resolution_note: Addressed by limiting the scope of claims to the observed support. Generalization beyond the panel remains unestablished.

criticisms.title: Visual analytics contribution may be seen as a software demo, not a research contribution
criticisms.criticism: A significant portion of the supplementary material consists of dashboard screenshots. Reviewers at computationally rigorous journals may view the visual analytics layer as a software demonstration rather than a scientific contribution. What evidence shows that the dashboard adds analytical value beyond what static figures provide?
artifact_evidence: Supplementary — Figures A4–A14 (dashboard screenshots)
journal_fit_targeting.json — 'auditable workflow' tagged as fit for EPJ
criticisms.rebuttal: The visual analytics layer is integral to the contribution, not ornamental: (1) It operationalizes regime-aware interpretation by allowing users to explore the bounded surface interactively, pinning parameter configurations and inspecting sensitivity at specific regime locations. (2) State serialization and PDF export create a reproducibility layer — any surface view can be exactly reconstructed from a state hash, unlike static plots that cannot be interrogated. (3) Support overlays and uncertainty diagnostics are coupled to the surface, making it impossible to inspect results without seeing their evidential boundaries. (4) The screenshots in the supplementary document the interface for review purposes but the actual contribution is the coupling of formal uncertainty diagnostics with interactive regime exploration. The dashboard is an analytical instrument, not a presentation tool.
corrective_actions: Supplementary introduces screenshots as 'interface documentation' not demonstration
State serialization described as reproducibility infrastructure (Section 6)
Support overlay coupling documented as analytical design feature
criticisms.resolution_note: Visual analytics framed as analytical instrument with reproducibility features, not as software demo.

criticisms.title: Construct validity of Z relies on six items and aggregate-level reliability
criticisms.criticism: Construct validity of Z rests on six WVS items, and the reported alpha is an aggregate-level statistic rather than a respondent-level psychometric estimate. Can this composite carry the paper’s central outcome?
artifact_evidence: rawdata/wvs_construct_audit.json — Z: 6 items, 287 cells, alpha=0.8187, unidimensional=true
main.tex Table 1 — construct audit with alpha, cells and usable items
criticisms.rebuttal: This criticism is the paper's own thesis, and the audit answers it with a measurement rather than an assertion. Z is built from its six configured items across 287 country-years and reaches alpha=0.8187, which clears the 0.70 floor the paper sets for itself; the other three candidate constructs fail the same test and are withdrawn. The paper also states the boundary: alpha here is an aggregate-level proxy, not a respondent-level psychometric estimate. What the audit cannot establish — that Z tracks belief rather than its WVS operationalisation — is named as the limitation that an independent outcome measure would resolve.
corrective_actions: construct_validity_invariance.json provides full psychometric diagnostics
Temporal invariance flagged for 2006/2018 instability
Discussion §8.3 identifies multi-item construct extension
Year-level instability documented in supplementary
criticisms.resolution_note: Resolved by the construct audit itself: alpha=0.8187 over 287 cells clears the stated floor, and the aggregate-level nature of the statistic is disclosed as a boundary rather than presented as a respondent-level estimate.

criticisms.title: Nine countries exceed the country-level MAE threshold; joint influence is untested
criticisms.criticism: The current country-alignment artifact reports MAE above 0.25 for 9 of 83 countries; six of the 34 preset countries are among them (CHN, CZE, FRA, GEO, ITA, POL). Several high-error countries contribute few observations. Does simultaneous exclusion of the preset cases materially change the fitted results?
artifact_evidence: preset_country_alignment.json — 9 all-country failures and 6 preset failures at MAE>0.25; 83 countries in the panel
paper/supplementary/supplementary_materials.tex Table S9 — preset-country and broader country-alignment diagnostics
criticisms.rebuttal: The year-averaged country-alignment artifact identifies six preset high-error cases and nine cases across all countries. These descriptive alignment results do not determine whether simultaneous exclusion changes model estimates. The manuscript flags joint exclusion of the six preset cases as a future sensitivity analysis; no joint-exclusion result is claimed.
corrective_actions: Current manuscript and supplement name the six preset cases and report the all-country threshold count
Single-country country-out evaluation is reported separately
Joint exclusion of the six preset cases remains an unrun sensitivity extension
criticisms.resolution_note: Partially disclosed. The simultaneous-exclusion sensitivity remains open, so the influence of the six preset cases on fitted results is not established.

criticisms.title: Repository lacks LICENSE file — compliance gap for open science
criticisms.criticism: A prior repository snapshot lacked a LICENSE file. Does the current repository still have that code/document licensing gap?
artifact_evidence: LICENSE — code and documentation license terms
data_code_provenance.json — third-party data restrictions are separate from the repository license
criticisms.rebuttal: The current repository contains a LICENSE file covering repository code and documentation. That license does not grant rights to redistribute third-party WVS/EVS, EM-DAT, OECD, or derived data; those permissions remain separate review items.
corrective_actions: Repository LICENSE file is present
Third-party source and derived-data terms remain tracked separately in data_code_provenance.json
criticisms.resolution_note: The repository-level LICENSE gap is closed. Third-party data permissions and derived-panel redistribution review remain outside this criticism and are still open.

author_response_pack.purpose: Concise anticipated reviewer concerns response for author use during submission and rebuttal
author_response_pack.general_strategy: Lead with transparency: the paper's primary defense is radical disclosure of limitations. For each criticism, point to the specific artifact, table, or section where the limitation is already documented. Frame the contribution as a reproducible, auditable methodology under explicitly stated constraints, not as a universal empirical finding.

top_5_attack_surfaces.one_line_defense: Rolling-origin is a 25-fold temporal scope diagnostic; mean interval coverage is 86.7%/84.5%/81.7% for Tiers A/B/C and does not validate temporal forecasting.

top_5_attack_surfaces.surface: Thin effective support for multi-parameter tiers
top_5_attack_surfaces.one_line_defense: The current 207-row panel yields support ratios of 18.82/11.50/9.41; Tier C remains exploratory and x_safe is below the Tier B stability threshold.

top_5_attack_surfaces.surface: No established predictive advantage over the linear baseline
top_5_attack_surfaces.one_line_defense: Grouped k-fold median R² ties at four decimals; the linear model fits better in sample, so predictive or functional-form superiority is not claimed.

top_5_attack_surfaces.surface: Restricted inputs and derived-panel redistribution review
top_5_attack_surfaces.one_line_defense: The runbook documents source retrieval and provenance, but clean-clone regeneration and redistribution clearance remain open; no legal clearance is claimed.

top_5_attack_surfaces.surface: Country-level high-error cases and untested joint exclusion
top_5_attack_surfaces.one_line_defense: The current alignment artifact reports 9 of 83 countries above MAE 0.25, including 6 preset countries; joint exclusion remains an unrun sensitivity analysis.

response_templates.temporal_instability: We agree that the current evidence does not establish temporal extrapolation. Repeated grouped k-fold is the primary spatial evaluation; country-out is a separate stress test, and rolling-origin is a temporal scope diagnostic. The current 25-fold rolling-origin analysis has mean 95% interval coverage of 86.7%/84.5%/81.7% for Tiers A/B/C, with 36%/48%/48% of folds below nominal. We report these results as limitations rather than forecasting validation.
response_templates.thin_support: The current panel has 207 unique country-years. Nominal support ratios are 18.82/11.50/9.41 observations per parameter for Tiers A/B/C. Tier A/B are the primary complexity tiers and Tier C is exploratory. The Tier B country-out stability summary has 83 folds and x_safe consistency of 0.759, below the 0.80 threshold; because the summary includes neutralized entries, it is not evidence that all terms are identified. Thin support remains a limitation.
response_templates.coverage_gap: The 95% intervals do not achieve nominal coverage consistently. Mean country-out coverage is 91.6%/91.4%/90.8% for Tiers A/B/C; rolling-origin means are 86.7%/84.5%/81.7%, and 36%/48%/48% of rolling folds fall below nominal. The manuscript reports protocol-specific coverage and variability and does not present these intervals as universally calibrated.
response_templates.novelty: We acknowledge that Hill/saturation modeling has a long history (Hill 1910, Michaelis-Menten 1913) and do not claim functional-form novelty. Our contribution is integrative: the combination of (a) regime-aware bounded modeling with (b) a protocolized multi-tier validation ladder, (c) deterministic reproducibility infrastructure with artifact versioning and claim-evidence traceability, and (d) coupled visual analytics that make support, uncertainty, and regime structure jointly visible. This integration for macro-urban social science panels under thin support is, to our knowledge, novel.
response_templates.ecological_fallacy: We explicitly acknowledge the ecological inference limitation throughout the manuscript (Discussion §8.1, citing Robinson 1950 and Openshaw 1984). The country-year is the intended unit of analysis, consistent with macro-urban analytics. All claims are framed as 'macro-level regularities in the fitted model' — no individual-level behavioral claims are made or implied.
response_templates.redistribution: The repository includes a derived panel and documents source provenance, but the upstream WVS/EVS data remain restricted and derived-panel redistribution review is unresolved. A clean clone cannot independently rebuild all inputs. The manuscript and runbook should describe that limitation without claiming redistribution clearance.
response_templates.country_errors: The current preset_country_alignment.json reports 9 of 83 countries above MAE 0.25, including six preset cases. These are descriptive country-alignment results. A simultaneous exclusion analysis has not been run, so the influence of the six cases is not established.

manuscript_update_recommendations.location: Supplementary correction note and C-withdrawal sensitivity discussion
manuscript_update_recommendations.recommendation: State clearly that the prior outcome–C identity arose in the defective earlier panel; in the current panel C is withdrawn/neutralized, so its exclusion and permutation results do not estimate a substantive C effect.
Keep the joint-exclusion sensitivity for CHN+CZE+FRA+GEO+ITA+POL as an open extension; do not imply that single-country LOO establishes the effect of excluding them together.
